newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hamas leader says only bombs can stop Israel.
newsitem.headline: Hamas leader says only bombs can stop Israel.

text.p: A Hamas leader freed by the Palestinian Authority last week said on Friday that only bombs could stop Israel from building a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

In a speech to a rally organised by a political party linked to the Hamas Islamic Resistance Movement, Ibrahim al-Makadmeh called for a new uprising against Israeli rule and vowed to make Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu regret his actions.
The rally was scheduled before a suspected Moslem suicide bomber killed two people at a Tel Aviv cafe on Friday.

"We must have the control and the power to stop the bulldozers of the enemy -- our unarmed people will not prevent it but the holy warriors carrying explosives on their shoulders and exploding the enemies of God (will)," Makadmeh told the crowd, estimated by journalists at about 10,000.

"We have to make Netanyahu curse the day in which he was born," he said, constantly interrupted by chants for Hamas's military wing the Izz el-Deen al-Qassam, which carried out a series of suicide bombings in Israel in the past.
Netanyahu called the release of leaders like Makadmeh a green light to bombers.

Neither Makadmeh nor any other speaker at the rally took responsibility for the Tel Aviv bombing on behalf of Hamas. But an anonymous caller to Israeli police said the Islamic Resistance Movement Hamas was responsible for the attack.
Hamas leaders in the West Bank refused to confirm or deny that the group carried out the attack.

Makadmeh, a 45-year-old dentist, was held for one year in a Palestinian Authority jail on suspicion of leading a secret group within Hamas dedicated to weakening Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's administration.
He spent nine years in an Israeli prison for his links to an Islamic group that preceded the founding of Hamas in 1987.

Palestinian police prevented busloads of supporters from attending the rally in the south of the Gaza Strip after news of the Tel Aviv attack but the meeting went ahead with those people who were already there.

"We need a new intifada, an intifada of a different kind," Makadmeh told the crowd, referring to the Palestinian revolt that erupted in 1987 and tapered off after Israel and the PLO signed a self-rule deal in 1993.
